A create names its Include and its Exclude by the tenant's names; a correction names only what differs, with the values it adds or removes; the turn-on is two lines. baselineConflict.$comment: Shown on a step whose baseline source policy a review found self-contradictory (roadmap/baselineConflict.ts): one entry per reviewed source, named by that record, so the words follow the source policy and not a goal.
baselineConflict.adminPortalNonAdminScope:
The baseline says this policy should block non-admins from admin portals. But the policy it actually defines targets All users and excludes no administrator — by role, account, or group. If IAMAI followed the policy definition literally, it would lock every administrator out of the admin portals. If it followed the documentation, it would need exclusions the policy doesn't have.

IAMAI won't write instructions for either interpretation because one locks admins out and the other is incomplete. Nothing is wrong in your tenant. This step waits for the baseline author to publish a corrected version. The rest of the plan is unaffected.

readiness.$commentMeasureStrength: A readiness number is measured against the policy's own requirement (roadmap/methodReadiness.ts, over the step's effects), and was labelled by the goal's family. The device-registration policy requires the custom strength Modern MFA + TAP, which Authenticator does not satisfy, and its threshold read "At least 5% MFA-ready" and "when MFA readiness reaches 90%" beside the registration policy's "79% MFA-ready" on the same board: two numbers for two requirements under one label, and a reader acted on the larger one (R4-26, Jordan D4). Where the policies require a strength the family's words do not already say (plain MFA for mfa and guest, Phishing-resistant MFA for admin), the measure names it, by the tenant's own name for it. Each ends on "readiness", as the family's own measures do, so the row's threshold reads in the shape the date column and the plan header look for ("when … readiness reaches 90% (now 27%)").

readiness.$commentBlind: "It is not measured yet" is true and unactionable on its own. Sixteen policies of one tenant were parked behind three sources the scan could not read, and no sentence anywhere named which three or what would open them — a blind the reader could have cleared in five minutes. The source's name, the recorded reason, the permission that reads it and the licence it needs all exist already (graph/collect/registry.ts, the snapshot's own SourceState).

The licence clause (blindFixLicensed) stays only where the tenant lacks it: no account or consent reads a source the tenant is not licensed for.

The campaign prepares people the scan has seen sign in. On a tenant where most people never have, the gate counts them and the campaign cannot: eleven people measured, a cohort of two, a 90% threshold. The reader finished the named step, read "Nothing left to do", and the number had not moved a point — with no other action anywhere on the board. Said only where finishing the named step provably cannot reach the threshold.

connect.h1: Strengthen identity security with evidence about who could be affected.
connect.intro: IAMAI reads a Microsoft Entra tenant, compares it with a reviewed identity-security baseline, and writes a dated plan to help you close the gaps and see who each change affects. It is read-only and runs in this browser.

status.$comment: Task 032: the approved pack's status strip above the staged flow (docs/design/approved/connect-v3.html). It is a projection of the same progression the stages already carry — the stage with the next action, or nothing left to do — never a second reading of readiness. The quiet half is the current stage's own state line, so the strip and the step cannot disagree.

baseline.goal: Its aim is layered protection for a small organisation: MFA for everyone, phishing-resistant admins, constrained sessions and devices, and emergency access kept out of every policy as a backup you check and test.

limits: Direct Send and connector-based SMTP relay do not sign in with user accounts, so these logs do not inventory them. A legacy-authentication block targets password-based sign-ins, not every mail-sending device. Confirm the sending method and test important jobs with their owners.
Authentication that happens outside Entra (federation, third-party MFA, on-premises apps) is recorded as a sign-in but not as what the other system enforced.
Anything on a longer cycle than the records (the quarterly invoice run, the yearly renewal) has left no evidence yet, and a report-only window shorter than its cycle cannot show it either.
Credentials saved on equipment nobody has touched in years surface the day something blocks them; a walk through the comms room beats any report.
A partner's own tenant enforces for their people; IAMAI sees their sign-ins here, never their controls.

home.metaTitle: IAMAI — Microsoft Entra Conditional Access planner
home.metaDescription: Check who could be affected by your Microsoft Entra security changes. IAMAI reviews your tenant and helps you plan the work before you deploy.
home.h1: Know what needs attention before you change a policy.
home.siteLine: A policy can look right and still cause problems. IAMAI checks who has the required sign-in methods, whether the available records show they use them, and which exclusions or outside accounts need a closer look. Then it helps you plan the changes.
heroMeta: You review and make the changes
home.workHeading: See what needs doing, and what needs to happen first.
home.workLead: Start with the tenant you have. IAMAI compares it with the Defense in Depth baseline, shows the gaps it can assess, and puts the work in order.

work.text: Review policies, accounts, groups and the sign-in evidence Microsoft makes available to this tenant.
See what already meets the baseline, what needs attention, and who a change could affect.
Work through the prerequisites, review the instructions, and test changes before enforcing them.

home.baseline: IAMAI plans against Defense in Depth: Conditional Access policies, built by Jon Hope, a Microsoft MVP.
home.baselineGoal: It covers MFA, administrator access, devices, sessions and more. IAMAI helps you work through the parts that apply to your tenant and prepare for changes that could affect people’s access.
home.baselineNote: You can inspect the baseline version IAMAI uses. Where IAMAI cannot assess a control, the plan identifies the review you need to carry out.
home.catchesHeading: A few things worth checking before you deploy.

catches.label: Sign-in methods
catches.text: Someone has registered a strong method, but the available records do not show them using it.

catches.label: Emergency access
catches.text: A proposed policy may reach the accounts you rely on to recover access.

catches.label: Exclusions
catches.text: Accounts in an exclusion group need a review of why they are still exempt.

catches.label: Outside accounts
catches.text: Guests may need different preparation or follow-up before a change applies to them.

catches.label: Shared accounts
catches.text: A meeting-room or service account may need attention before new sign-in requirements take effect.

home.trustLabel: What it does with your tenant
home.trustHeading: Your tenant stays under your control.

trust.title: IAMAI does not change your tenant
trust.body: You can review the permissions before connecting. Approving them adds one enterprise application to the tenant, which you can delete. IAMAI reads the tenant to build the plan; you decide which changes to make and carry them out yourself.

trust.title: Your scan is processed on your device
trust.body: Tenant data is read from Microsoft and processed in your browser. IAMAI has no server, so your scan is not uploaded anywhere. Downloaded plans and copied briefings can contain tenant information, so review them before sharing. The website host may also collect page-load information.

trust.title: You can inspect the code
trust.body: The source and documented limits are public. Check how IAMAI works, report a problem, or suggest an improvement.

home.aboutHeading: Built by someone who does this work.
home.about: I’m Lachlan Robinette. I work with Microsoft Entra security baselines across MSP-managed tenants. I built IAMAI to help with the checks and decisions that sit between a baseline and a successful rollout. It is still in public preview. If something is wrong or unclear, tell me at feedback@getiamai.com.

plan.$commentNoOperationCovered: "This step has no policy for IAMAI to write in this plan. Scan again to rebuild it." was said over a step whose own record names the tenant policy already delivering the goal (Step.satisfiedBy). Both halves are wrong for that case: there is nothing to rebuild, and rescanning changes nothing, so a reader scanned, got the identical page, and had no way forward. Two clauses, not a paragraph (owner, 2026-09-22): the policy, so the reader can check IAMAI matched the right one, and that nothing is coming. What is still open is the Readiness tiles above and the completion below, and repeating it here is fluff.
plan.noOperationCovered: {policy} found. IAMAI writes no policy here.
plan.$commentNoOperationHeld: "This step has no policy for IAMAI to write in this plan. Scan again to rebuild it." was said over an update with nothing in it, because the tenant's policy already holds every section the step writes (Action.nothingOwed). Both halves were false: the policy is there, and every scan rebuilt the same empty update. Following the plan reaches it: the demo tenants' compliant-device policy, enforced as the step asked, is then read as narrower than the baseline in its device platforms. It names the policy, so the reader can check IAMAI matched the right one, and says nothing is coming; no rescan is promised, because none changes it. noOperationHeldGap follows where the goal is still short in a condition, which no update writes: {gaps} is the classifier's own sentence (engine.coverage.reason.conditionsNarrower), one per policy, joined with semicolons. noOperation stays for a step with no operations at all, such as one loaded from an older plan file, where a scan does rebuild it.
plan.noOperationHeld: Everything this step writes is already in {policy}, so IAMAI has nothing to submit here.
plan.$commentSwitchedOff: A policy this plan is tracking that the tenant has switched off is not a policy to create: it exists, and creating one makes a second. `claimedPolicy` will not take a disabled policy as the live one, so the step fell through to "Create the policy in Report-only" on a policy already sitting in the tenant. It reproduces whenever somebody switches a policy off after it breaks something, and on an inherited tenant that arrives with one off. The change is Report-only, never straight to On (owner, 2026-09-23: "We only want one set of report-only. If someone has to revert and turns it off, we should advise placing it to Report-only, and then they switch it on when they are ready and data supports it."). It said "set Enable policy to On", which enforces the moment it is saved with no report-only watch before it. Report-only denies nobody, so nothing the plan waits on before a turn-on holds this; the next scan finds the policy in Report-only and the step's ordinary watch and readiness gates decide the turn-on.
plan.switchedOff: {policy} is already in {tenant} and switched off. Setting it to Report-only is the change here, not a new policy and not On: open it in the Entra admin center, check its settings still match this step, and set Enable policy to Report-only. IAMAI then watches it there, and this step says when it can be turned on.

A pair with one member Off reads switchedOff, naming that member. Read off the step's own policy alone, a pair was never read as switched off: with one member Off it handed over a batch that created both guest policies again, and once its gates cleared a PATCH that took the Off one straight to On; with both Off it said to create the two guest policies.

IAMAI then watches them there, and this step says when they can be turned on.

Every account read and passing: the all-clear, worded as the configuration procedure's. Any account unread: that account named, and the procedure is for it if it has none.

A fact, not a check: it replaces the bg.notPersonal note on that card and gates nothing. Owner wording, 2026-09-23.

Nothing chosen: choose (or create, where no group exists). A group chosen: the missing emergency accounts to add, then the policies that do not yet exclude it, one by name or a count. plan.$commentRecoverySignIn: Verify Emergency Access: what an account's Sign-in evidence card, its print and its exports say while the account waits for a passkey sign-in (src/roadmap/emergencyJourney.ts recoveryWaitingLine).

recoverySignIn.$comment: One line each. The card read “Sign in with this account’s passkey after {date}. Last sign-in seen {date} did not count: …”, which asks for a sign-in at a time already past (owner, 2026-09-23). It asks for a sign-in since the most recent change and lists the two dates that show whether one has happened: when the account's recovery configuration last changed, and the latest sign-in IAMAI read for the account. The first is lastChange only for a change IAMAI read in the directory audit log; where that log shows none it is noChangeSince. The last sign-in is of any kind. A reason stays only where the dates cannot show it: a sign-in after the change that still did not qualify.
recoverySignIn.since: Sign in with this account’s passkey since the most recent change.
recoverySignIn.$commentSinceNone: The first line where the directory audit log IAMAI read shows no change (noChangeSince below): it asks for the sign-in without naming a change the next line says was not seen.
recoverySignIn.sinceNone: Sign in with this account’s passkey.
recoverySignIn.$commentNoChangeSince: Where the directory audit log IAMAI read shows no change to the account's recovery configuration, the account's baseline starts where that log begins, about 30 days before the first scan that prepared it, and stays there until a change arrives. That date is not a change: “Last change: {date}” named one on a day nothing changed, which is the usual state of a tenant whose emergency access was set up long ago (review, 2026-09-23). Nothing relevant changed since this date, as far as the log IAMAI read shows.
recoverySignIn.$commentNotPasskey: The last sign-in is the account's last sign-in of any kind, not only its latest passkey sign-in: “Last sign-in” read passkey sign-ins only, so a password, Temporary Access Pass or Authenticator sign-in after the change showed as “none seen” or as an older passkey date, and sent the reader to log lag instead of to the method used (review, 2026-09-23). Added under a last sign-in after the change that is later than every passkey sign-in IAMAI read: a sign-in with another method, or a passkey attempt that failed (the sign-in log records no passkey proof for a failure).
recoverySignIn.notPasskey: That sign-in did not succeed with a passkey.
recoverySignIn.$commentRecordPending: A passkey sign-in since the change that meets every condition, while the account still waits: IAMAI records it from a scan (planData.ts reconcileAutomaticRecovery), so until then the card showed a last sign-in after the last change under the instruction to sign in, and the dates read as done (review, 2026-09-23). It asks for the scan, not another sign-in, and wins over notPasskey: a later sign-in with another method does not undo it.
recoverySignIn.recordPending: Scan again to record the passkey sign-in.
recoverySignIn.$commentUnconfigured: Before IAMAI has observed a verified configuration there is no change to date, so the line waits for the checks instead.
recoverySignIn.unconfigured: Sign in with this account’s passkey once the configuration checks pass.
recoverySignIn.$commentMilestone: Verify Emergency Access's line under its milestone while an account still has to sign in (cleanupExport.ts drillMilestone), in place of "Verify every selected account after the final configuration is observed.". Owner wording, 2026-09-23.
recoverySignIn.milestone: Sign in with each emergency access account.

stepContract.$comment: The Step Contract (Foundation D, src/ui/surfaces/stepContract.ts). Every Plan step answers the same questions in the same order: where it is now and what happens next, why, what IAMAI found, who it touches, what to do, what to fix first, how you will know it is done, and More. These are the words the contract itself supplies; each step's own sentences stay in its steps[] entry.

kind.$comment: The opened step's eyebrow (task 034; docs/design/approved/plan-step-v1.html draws `Policy step` and `Resolution step` above the title). One label per steps[].kind, so the label names what production already calls the step rather than a second taxonomy. A kind with no entry here shows no eyebrow.

stepContract.$commentCardMore: The fold on a Tasks Remaining card that names people: the first five are named on the card, the rest under this (ContentStep.tsx, whoBlocks.ts NAMES_INLINE).
stepContract.$commentCardPerson: A person on a Tasks Remaining card, with MFA Readiness's own next step for them (ui/surfaces/personNext.ts; owner 2026-09-24: the Plan and MFA Readiness speak one language, and every direction names the method).

The name is Step.satisfiedBy — the coverage result that decided the goal was satisfied — so the rail names the tenant's own policy and never the baseline's. `railExistingKeep` is the sub under one sufficient policy; `railExistingTogether` is the sub where two cover the goal between them and neither covers it alone.
stepContract.railExistingKeep: Nothing to create; keep it as it is.
stepContract.railExistingTogether: Together — neither covers the goal on its own.

It restates `implementationReady` in the pack's grammar and adds no fact — the channels stand or fall together on Foundation A's one answer (roadmap/operations.ts implementationOffered), so a step that offers none shows `implementationNone` instead and no list at all.

foundLabel.$comment: The key over each finding card (task 035; docs/design/approved/plan-step-v1.html `.finding .k`). It names which KIND of finding this is — the classification stepContract.ts foundOf already makes when it builds the list — and never restates the finding's own sentence.

stepContract.foundReadiness: Enforcement waits for {measure} to reach {threshold}; it is {value} today.
stepContract.foundReadinessFloor: Enforcement waits for {measure} to reach {threshold}. At least {value} are ready: {line}

The count is computed (roadmap/methodReadiness.ts) and was rendered nowhere.
stepContract.foundReadinessUnmeasured: Enforcement waits for {measure} to reach {threshold}. It is not measured yet: {line}
stepContract.foundEnforcedShort: This policy is enforced, and {line} Anyone it does not accept is refused where it applies until they register a method it does.
stepContract.$commentFoundEnforcedUnmeasured: The readiness gate is computed only for an unfinished step, so a policy enforced in the portal while IAMAI was holding it back lost every trace of the hold. A reader enforced the admin policy with neither admin's method readable (the registration source was 403); the step read Completed, its Done-when satisfied, and nothing said the threshold had never been met - a gate that congratulates you for walking around it. The finished step now states the threshold and that nothing showed it met. It holds nothing: the work is done, and this is a fact about the tenant. It claims nothing about WHEN the policy went on, which IAMAI cannot know for a policy it found already enforced.
stepContract.foundEnforcedUnmeasured: This policy is enforced. The plan holds enforcement until {measure} reaches {threshold}, and IAMAI cannot measure it, so nothing has shown that threshold met. Anyone it does not accept is refused where it applies until they register a method it does.

Owner, 2026-09-24 (walk list 4.x item 10 and L4): they no longer hold the step's 90% gate, which counts the people MFA Readiness counts; whoever signs in to one first registers its method, so the step names them and where to disable them. Up to twenty by name; past that, the step that disables them lists them.

Owner, 2026-09-24 (walk list 4.x item 43): one heading in every state, the account named, and the step that fixes it. It was headed "Before turning on" in one state and "Prerequisites" in another, over "Your safe way in · when 1 safe way in for the signed-in account exists (now 0)".

Both end on the step that gets them ready, and link to it. It replaced "Enforcement waits for {measure} to reach {threshold}; it is {value} today." and "…; it waits on X, which is where to start" on these gates: the row and the value state the threshold.

methodGate.everyoneValue: {ready} of {total} people have a method it accepts

stepContract.$commentFoundEnforcedUnwatched: Owner decision 3 (2026-09-22; R4-12, Jordan D7): a finished policy this plan owns (its tag on the satisfying policy, enforced) that went live with no report-only period IAMAI watched stays Completed, and its Readiness says so on a warning tile (ui/surfaces/doneWhen.ts enforcedUnwatched: IAMAI watched every policy member go On from not deployed at the scan before, or from Off on the same object after a scan that recorded it not deployed, with no report-only state between, and the scan's sign-in records show no report-only result for it, observation.ts skippedWindow). A record must have seen the step's policy not deployed. Never on a policy a first scan found On or Off, which is also how a policy this plan built and watched through report-only reads from a second browser or after Forget: IAMAI cannot know that one skipped anything. Never on a different object replacing the one recorded, which the record only sighted and the scan before may have seen in report-only. Built straight to On, policies on the pinned baseline filed under Completed with the scan's sentence alone, and the one note saying nobody watched them sat under New evidence. This tile is that fact's one home on the step: the New evidence note that says the same (observations.appearedEnforced) is left out where it draws. It states what IAMAI could watch, never when the policy went on, which IAMAI cannot know. Never on a policy the tenant already had (In place): nothing went live under this plan there. The check after the change stays in the Done-when (shared.policyVerifyAfter), and this sentence does not repeat it.

followUp.campaignOpen: The policies go ahead without {names} once everyone else is ready. Give each a Temporary Access Pass when they can register.

drift.setBackTasks: Set {dimension} back as Implementation Tasks shows.

readinessRoute.$comment: Where a readiness number is moved, by its family (copy/reasons.ts READINESS_MEASURE), for a measure the plan itself has no step for. A family with no entry states the number alone.
readinessRoute.device: Device readiness moves in Intune, not here: enroll the devices on the chosen platforms and assign a compliance policy, then scan again. No step of this plan enrolls a device for you.

stepContract.$commentFoundReadinessRouteStep: A gate that says what it waits for but not what opens it is half a sentence. The plan already knows: generate.ts draws the edge from a readiness-held step to the campaign that moves the number, and the step it drew to was named nowhere on the held step. Only where that edge exists.
stepContract.foundReadinessRouteStep: The step that moves this number is “{step}”.
stepContract.$commentFoundReadinessRouteStepHeld: The same pointer where the step it names cannot be done today (R4-33, Marcus D15). The Threshold card sent the reader to Prepare Your Team for MFA, which sat On Hold behind Register Your Own Passkey, which was Up Next behind Verify Emergency Access: three hops across three tabs to find the first thing anybody could do. The board's own lane readings know the chain: the sentence names the first step on it that is Ready, and the card links there.
stepContract.foundReadinessRouteStepHeld: The step that moves this number is “{step}”; it waits on “{first}”, which is where to start.

readinessValue.$comment: The threshold tile's collapsed value, by its measure's family (copy/reasons.ts READINESS_MEASURE): the percentage and what it measures (content review S3). A family with no entry shows the percentage alone.
readinessValue.device: {value} of people on a compliant device

stepContract.foundInPlace: {tenant} already has a policy doing this, so there is nothing to create.
stepContract.foundInPlaceNamed: Already delivered by {policies}, so there is nothing to create.
stepContract.$commentFoundShortfall: A goal can be delivered and still miss most of the directory. coverage.ts records who it does not reach and why, for every goal, and the sentence never reached a surface: a policy excluding a group that holds 116 of 122 accounts read "already delivered, so there is nothing to create" beside "6 active people", with nothing naming the gap.
stepContract.foundShortfall: This goal is written for {active} people in this tenant; {n} of them are excluded from the policy that delivers it, so it reaches {reached}.
stepContract.$commentFoundWider: A step named for one group offering to create a policy that reaches everybody. "Require MFA for Guests", on a tenant with one guest, offered the baseline's tenant-wide MFA policy under a name that promised guests: follow it and you apply MFA to the whole company from a step named for one guest. Disclosure, not substitution — two Foundation A invariants say the goal's population must never decide which policy is built, and they are right.
stepContract.foundWider: This step is named for {cohort}, and the policy it would create applies to everyone in the tenant. That is the baseline source IAMAI matched to this goal, and it is not narrowed to {cohort}. Read its assignments before you create it.

foundWiderCohort.$comment: The cohort a step is named for, by the goal's expectedWho kind (data/goals.json). Only the kinds for which a tenant-wide policy is a real widening appear: members is mapped to one by the baseline author on purpose.

stepContract.$commentFoundDiffers: The deployed policy is not what this step asked for, in a part IAMAI writes. The comparison existed and its answer was discarded after deciding readiness, so a policy built with a narrowing condition left at Configure: No — the trap the step's own procedure warns about — rendered identically to one built exactly right.
stepContract.$commentFoundTaggedDisabled: A tenant IAMAI has planned before arrives carrying policies with IAMAI's own plan tag, and one of them is switched off. The engine matches it (tracking.matchedBy is a tag, tracking.state is disabled) and then ignores it, because a disabled policy cannot be the step's live policy — so the step proposed a second policy of the same name, the operator built it, two policies then carried the tag for one step, and the step could never finish. The proposal no longer suffixes around the step's own policy, and the finding says what is there. It renders only where another reason holds the step first, and it ended "or follow the instructions below and leave it switched off": there, the instructions below were the create procedure, so following them built a second policy beside the one that is Off. The step's own procedure for that policy is now the Report-only one, and the finding no longer points anywhere else.
stepContract.foundTaggedDisabled: {policy} already carries this step's tag in {tenant} and is switched off, so it is doing nothing today. IAMAI does not turn a policy on: review its settings in the Entra admin center and, if it is the one you want, set Enable policy to Report-only there, not On.
stepContract.$commentFoundDiffersResources: Which resources, where the resources are what differs (stepContract.ts foundOf, tracking.ts resourcesDiffer; net-new 14): 4.4's read only "target resources differ" where the baseline excludes Microsoft Intune Enrollment and the tenant's policy does not.
stepContract.$commentFoundWatched: A step IAMAI WATCHED move is not a report of coverage that was already there (stepContract.ts foundOf, observation.ts since === 'observed-change'). Saying "already delivered ... so there is nothing to create" on the step somebody has just created, watched for a week and enforced erases their work and describes it as a policy they never needed to build.
stepContract.foundInPlaceWatched: {policies} is in place. IAMAI watched it get there.
stepContract.foundInPlaceWatchedTogether: {policies} are in place together, and no one of them covers the whole goal on its own. IAMAI watched them get there.
stepContract.foundInPlaceTogether: Already delivered by {policies} together — none of them covers the whole goal on its own — so there is nothing to create.
stepContract.doneSatisfied: The scan found the assessed configuration in place.
stepContract.$commentPolicyFact: What a policy in Turn On MFA for Everyone does, read from the policy IAMAI will see (ui/surfaces/policyFact.ts): the policy the step writes while it is open, and the tenant policy that delivers it once done. Its Satisfied card states it (walk list 4.x item 22: "On · Requires MFA for All users except Core - Exclusions"), its Completion Criteria's first line (item 26) and its AI Info lead (item 31). verbs holds each verb in the third person and as a participle; controls names the built-in grant controls a fact can state. A policy with anything these words cannot say gets no fact.

policyFact.$commentAdminRoles: A role list the fact would count reads as admin roles, with no number: the create task beside it counts the baseline's roles, and the tenant's own policy can hold more (owner, 2026-09-24: 4.3 read 133 beside 46).

policyFact.$commentFactWhen: A policy in Extend MFA Coverage applies at a moment, not to every sign-in (owner, 2026-09-25: section 5 finishes on 4.x's two lines): the registration it protects, the risk it answers, the authentication context or the application it is scoped to. A condition with no words here gives no fact at all (ui/surfaces/policyFact.ts whenOf).

It read its milestone, "No change needed.", over a tile saying Could not verify: on the Follow-up snapshot Configure Passkey Settings said so over "Existing passkeys affected - Could not verify", whose note said some registered authentication methods were not readable. An absolute all-clear over a check IAMAI could not make is a claim it cannot know; this scopes the all-clear to what was read and names the check that was not. stepContract.$commentFixStepAt: A prerequisite is not always waited on until it is FINISHED (src/actionability/dependency-data.json carries the milestone on every edge). Turn Off Security Defaults waits for the replacement policies to be ready to enforce; those policies wait for it to be complete. Both tiles said "Finish the other first", so the pair read as a deadlock that the data does not contain — and the way out of an apparent deadlock is to turn security defaults off, which is the one thing the step's own words say not to do yet. A null milestone draws no note under the card: Turn Off Security Defaults' own card already says to turn them off the day the four policies below it are ready (walk list 4.x item 50).

hardening.$commentLeadAdvisory: The lead of a finished emergency step whose open recommendation is not one the plan tracks (R4-56). leadDefer promises a Defer control and a Cleanup row, and those exist only for the hardening the step's own tally counts (step.emergency.hardening). The checks about the credential itself - accounts sharing an Authenticator device, every account on one method type, a synced passkey only - are shown on Prepared passkeys and hold nothing, so the step read "Fix these, or defer them: ... they stay in Cleanup until they pass" over no defer control, no list and no Cleanup row. This says what is true: the minimum is met, the rollout does not wait on it, and where the recommendation is. "This does not hold the rollout" is true of the code, not yet the owner's rule: validation/emergencyTiers.ts says the rollout waits on resilience hardening until it is fixed or deferred, and whether these credential checks count in the tally is an open owner question (R4-56). If they are counted, leadDefer covers them and this sentence is removed.

implementation.$commentReference: A finished step still draws its Implementation Tasks on purpose: with nothing needing doing, every change stays available to look up. Observations, saved choices, proposals and unknowns are kept apart; never confirmation that a change was made.
aiFacts.heading: IAMAI FACTS FOR THIS STEP
aiFacts.boundary: What follows is what IAMAI observed in this tenant's latest scan and what its plan proposes. It does not confirm that any change has been made.

opening: Help me understand and carry out this IAMAI step. Explain its purpose, who it affects, how the tenant's observed state compares with the intended result, and what remains to do. Use the facts below; distinguish observations, saved decisions, proposed changes and unknowns.

Explain the next available action first, then the settings and checks needed to complete it. Point out any conflict between the instructions and the supplied policy data. If Microsoft behavior needs clarification, use current Microsoft documentation and cite the relevant page. Do not invent tenant values, approvals, completed checks or changes. Ask only for information that affects the next action.

You may explain alternatives and their tradeoffs. Clearly identify any alternative that changes the selected baseline or saved decision, and do not present it as the current plan. Do not execute a tenant change from this briefing.
aiFacts.previewValues: Values shown as ‹…› are not resolved yet. Do not run this output.

implementation.channelUnavailable: This format has no output for the current action. Use the available guidance and readiness checks on this step.

inPlace: The tenant already delivers this, so nothing is generated for it.
observe: No tenant change to submit right now
The policy stays in report-only while IAMAI observes it.
decision: Answer the question this step is waiting on first.
unavailable: No artifact for this policy yet

conflict: Not enough information to provide implementation guidance.
The baseline defines this policy two ways. Until the baseline author publishes a corrected version, no implementation steps are available.

bindingMissing: IAMAI does not yet hold every value this change needs, so no artifact is produced.
confirmationsPending: IAMAI cannot read these from Microsoft. Confirm them under Readiness, and the enforcement artifacts appear here.
packageFault: This step's implementation content could not be projected safely, so no artifact is offered.
correctionUnknown: IAMAI found a difference on this policy that the step’s corrections do not cover, so no partial correction is offered.

emails.subject: Subject: {subject}

s-goal-all-users-no-persistence.subject: Changes to Work Browser Sign-ins
s-goal-all-users-no-persistence.body: We are updating browser sign-in settings to reduce the risk of work accounts staying signed in on shared or unattended computers. After the change, you may need to sign in again when you reopen your browser. Keep your approved sign-in method available. Save work before closing the browser and always sign out on shared computers. If you encounter repeated prompts or cannot access a work app, contact IT with the app name and the time of the problem.

s-goal-mfa-all-users.subject: Stronger Sign-in Protection for Your Work Account
s-goal-mfa-all-users.body: We are strengthening sign-in protection for work accounts. Make sure you have registered an approved authentication method at https://aka.ms/mfasetup and can use it to sign in. Contact IT before the change if you need help registering or cannot use the offered methods. We will confirm the rollout date separately.

s-goal-admin-session.subject: Review Administrator Session Settings
s-goal-admin-session.body: We are reviewing sign-in session settings for administrator accounts. Test your normal administrative tasks and tell IT about any unexpected prompts or interrupted work so we can coordinate the change.

s-goal-inforcer-mfa.subject: MFA for Inforcer Access
s-goal-inforcer-mfa.body: We are reviewing MFA protection for Inforcer access. Please confirm your work account has an approved MFA method and contact IT if you need help testing sign-in. Tell IT about any unattended job that uses a person’s account so its access path can be reviewed separately.

s-ladder-legacy-auth-inventory.subject: Review Older Sign-In Workflows
s-ladder-legacy-auth-inventory.body: Please identify each application, printer or scheduled job that uses an older client or username-and-password protocol. Include the account, actual protocol, owner, normal and infrequent run schedules, supported replacement and a delivery or access test window.

s-ladder-app-passwords.subject: Coordinate App Password Retirement
s-ladder-app-passwords.body: Please identify applications or jobs that use an app password. Arrange a supported replacement and test access with IT before removing the old credential. Confirm the app password has been removed and report any failed workflow so we can finish the change.

s-prereq-exclusion-group.subject: Review Emergency Exclusions
s-prereq-exclusion-group.body: Please review the emergency-access group and its membership, and confirm the exclusions on the listed existing policies. Let us know if another approved exception needs to remain.

s-prereq-service-accounts-group.subject: Confirm Service Account Use
s-prereq-service-accounts-group.body: Please confirm the jobs each listed account runs. Identify temporary mail exceptions separately from other service access the account still needs. We will use the confirmed list to prepare the group and check its policy scope.

s-prereq-auth-strength.subject: Review Authentication Strength Setup
s-prereq-auth-strength.body: Please review the required authentication methods and model restrictions, together with the policies that use this strength. Identify any working method the proposed settings would exclude, and suggest a change window if adjustments are needed.

s-prereq-allowed-countries.subject: Confirm Work Countries
s-prereq-allowed-countries.body: Please confirm the countries where people normally work and the recurring travel destinations listed below. Recurring travel is recorded separately from the normal-work access policy. Please send any corrections.

s-prereq-trusted-location.subject: Confirm Office Networks
s-prereq-trusted-location.body: Please confirm which of the listed named networks belong to our offices. If an office is missing, provide its public egress IP range and location name so we can create the named location in Entra. If everyone works remotely, confirm that instead.

s-prereq-device-plan.subject: Confirm Device Access Requirements
s-prereq-device-plan.body: Please review our proposed phone management, phone app protection and computer management choices below. Identify work apps or devices that need a different arrangement, and confirm who will prepare the required device and app settings.

s-check-dormant-accounts.subject: Review Inactive Accounts
s-check-dormant-accounts.body: Please review the listed accounts and last-known activity. Confirm which accounts are still needed and why, which can be disabled, and which need investigation.

s-check-separate-admin-accounts.subject: Plan Separate Administrator Access
s-check-separate-admin-accounts.body: Please confirm the ordinary and dedicated administrator accounts for the people listed below. We need to test that each dedicated account can perform the required work before removing administrative access from the ordinary account. Please suggest a handover time.

s-shared-devices.subject: Test Shared Device Access
s-shared-devices.body: Please review the shared accounts and proposed policy scope below. The device owner needs to test the normal work tasks and sign-in flow before and after the change. Please confirm who will perform the test and report any interruption.

s-goal-guests-mfa.subject: Upcoming Guest MFA Requirements
s-goal-guests-mfa.body: We are strengthening MFA requirements for guest access to our organization. Please review the proposed access change with your team and confirm which guest accounts you use. We will coordinate a test before changing access. If you encounter a sign-in problem, contact IT with the affected account and time of the attempt.

s-goal-block-legacy-auth.subject: Review Older Sign-In and Email Methods
s-goal-block-legacy-auth.body: We are preparing to block older username-and-password sign-in methods. Please identify applications, printers or scanners that still depend on them, and confirm the authentication and TLS capabilities, sender and recipient requirements, and a delivery-test window for each. SMTP with OAuth, connector-based relay and Direct Send use different paths; please provide the actual method your device uses.

workflows.generic: Identify what the policy protects, who it includes and excludes, and which access requirements it applies.
reviewInstructions: Match every application, group, location and authentication strength in the baseline to the intended object in this tenant. Never reuse a baseline author’s tenant-specific IDs.
Check the policies already here, and exclude the emergency access accounts from anything that blocks or restricts sign-in. A report-only policy blocks nobody and needs no exclusion.

Test the exclusions as well as the rule: another policy can still ask an excluded person for MFA.
To back a change out, set the policy back to Report-only rather than delete it; a deleted one can be restored for 30 days and no longer.
Confirm that the intended access works and unwanted access is blocked. Record the review below only after you have validated the control; IAMAI does not verify completion of this manual step.

PIM role settings.why: Whether activating each role someone is eligible for asks for the authentication context Require MFA at Every Role Activation's policy targets.
PIM role settings.note: Read for each of those roles, after the roles themselves. A role whose read fails stays one to set.

Per-user MFA requirements.why: Each account's legacy per-user MFA state, whatever the authentication-methods migration says.
Per-user MFA requirements.note: Read for every account as the directory arrives. An account whose read fails stays unknown.

CA policies.why: The tenant's Conditional Access policies, which the plan compares with the baseline; Microsoft-managed policies are marked.

Named locations.why: The named locations the trusted-location and country checks read.

Authentication strengths.why: The strengths policies refer to, custom ones included, and the method combinations each allows.

Auth methods policy.why: Which sign-in methods are on and for whom, the passkey settings, whether registration is enforced, and whether the tenant has finished moving off the legacy MFA settings (read from beta when v1.0 leaves that out).
Auth methods policy.note: Read with Global Reader or Authentication Policy Administrator; a refused read also holds the passkey settings step.

Security defaults.why: Whether security defaults are on; they cannot be on alongside Conditional Access.

Device registration policy.why: Whether the tenant-wide device-registration MFA setting is on, which a Conditional Access policy on registering devices needs off.
Device registration policy.note: Read with Global Reader or a device administration role; with another role it reads as unknown, never as off.

Cross-tenant access.why: How accounts from other tenants are trusted, for the steps about guests and external access.

Role assignments.why: Who holds an active directory role, for the administrator steps, and the role names shown.

Role assignment schedules.why: Whether an active emergency administrator role is assigned permanently rather than eligible, activated or time-limited.

PIM eligibility.why: Roles held as eligible rather than active; an eligible role is outside a role-scoped policy until it is activated.

Subscribed SKUs.why: The licences the tenant holds and how many are assigned.

Organization.why: The tenant's name and verified domains, for the plan file's header.

Signed-in operator.why: Which account in the directory is yours. The emergency-account and passkey checks read it, and so do the steps that mention your own account.

Registration details.why: Which method types each person has registered, without phone numbers, for MFA readiness.

Users.why: Every account, with its last sign-in, licences and directory details.
Users.note: Last sign-in dates need Entra ID P1; without it the accounts are read without them.

Devices.why: Each device's compliance and join state and its registered owners, for the device steps.

SP sign-in activity.why: When each application identity last signed in, which shows the applications in use in this tenant.

Auth methods.why: Each account's registered methods, with the passkey model, type and attestation details; IAMAI keeps the details its checks need and never saves phone numbers.
Auth methods.note: An account whose methods cannot be read is read again on its own; one still unread stays unknown, and the registration report stands in for it.

App sign-in summary.why: Sign-in counts per application, for deciding which applications a policy should cover.

Sign-in logs.why: Interactive sign-ins, for predicting what a policy would do and for showing who has completed MFA.

Directory audit events.why: Each event's activity, category, result and the objects it changed, to date changes to the emergency accounts, their exclusions group, Conditional Access policies and the passkey policy.

how.hostingBody: IAMAI runs in your browser. It reads tenant data directly from Microsoft Graph and keeps the scan in this browser. On Connect it also asks GitHub (api.github.com, raw.githubusercontent.com) whether the baseline's author has published changes since the pinned version, and, when there are changes, reads the changed files; no tenant data is sent. The public source and site files are on GitHub Pages, served through Cloudflare. Hosting includes a Cloudflare page-load beacon, which is not in IAMAI's application bundle. IAMAI does not send the tenant snapshot to that beacon. Review exports before sharing them.

caps.$commentPim: Privileged Identity Management: Microsoft licenses it with Entra ID P2 or Microsoft Entra ID Governance, which P1 tenants buy without P2 (src/licensing/capabilities.ts, data/service-plans.json). It was read as Entra ID P2, so a P1 tenant holding Governance was told its eligible role assignments needed P2 and never had them read (R4-37). The Inventory licensing table names it with the other capabilities.

inventory.$commentNotRead: What an Inventory table says in place of its rows where the scan got nothing out of its section (graph/collect/coreSections.ts sectionHasData: a refusal, an error, a licence gate, or a section the scan lacks), with the section's own reason. The tables drew such a section as a finding: "Security defaults: off", every capability "not licensed", 0 MFA-capable, "No devices are registered.", "No named locations exist yet." and "135 built-in roles hidden: no holder", on scans where Connect listed the section as not read. The Export CSV card offers no file for such a table. A cell whose own source was not read says pages.connect.scan.gaps.notRead.
inventory.$commentTooLittle: The sign-in records where the read stopped short of the minimum it needs (graph/collect/laneBCore.ts, status insufficient): some records came back, so "not read" would be false, and too few to count from.

inventory.$commentPartlyRead: The line over a table whose section the scan read only in part (status partial and not a licence gate, as Connect's unread list reads it). The Sign-in countries tab said "nobody" used device-code sign-in over a read that covered 52 hours of the 30 days asked for, and never said the read stopped short.
inventory.$commentColumnNotRead: The line over a table drawn from one section while a column's own section was not read, or was read in part: the Apps table's sign-in counts are the app sign-in summary's and its last activity the service principals'. With the service principals' activity not read, the line said "Not read in this scan: Request failed (500)." as if the whole table were unread, and the screen drew "—" in Last activity where the CSV wrote "not read". {column} is the column's header.

The note said those roles had "no holder", and on a tenant licensed for PIM an eligible Global Administrator is the ordinary case. {roles} is the count of built-in roles hidden, through count() as the note it stands in for (copy/inventory.ts roles.hiddenNote): a bare {n} stood before a fixed plural.

It said "(/reports, 30 days). Detected workloads drive which goals apply." The Detected workloads word is what the scan saw of each service (roadmap/workflows.ts serviceReading), and an app service's facet is on whatever the scan saw (coverage/applicability.ts detectFacets, FACET_APPS), so demo read "Inforcer | not seen" under a tip saying that drove the goals while its Plan carried the Inforcer MFA step. The sources state no window (see serviceEvidence $commentSeen), so none is named.

inventory.$commentUnnamedObjects: How the Inventory names a group, a named location or an authentication strength the directory holds no name for, by its kind (ui/surfaces/inventoryTables.ts objectLabels). Every one read "an unnamed account": a method scoped to the emergency-access group read "Passkey or FIDO2 security key | enabled | an unnamed account", and a country block read "locations: all except an unnamed account" on a scan that could not read named locations. Plainly, never as a phrase about IAMAI (names.ts, walk-51 item 4); a location or strength whose section was not read says so.

inventory.strengthNotRead: an authentication strength that was not read
inventory.$commentTargetsExcept: The Authentication tab's Targets cell where a method excludes groups (the method's excludeTargets, as Graph returns them): {include} is the targets it reaches, {exclude} the groups it leaves out. The cell read only the included targets, so a passkey method for all users that excluded the emergency-access group read "All users" while Emergency Access, reading the same policy, said those accounts could not use a passkey.
inventory.$commentAuthenticatorMode: The Microsoft Authenticator row of the Authentication table: each target with the authentication mode Graph returns for it (any, push, deviceBasedPush), by the portal's names (roadmap/portalLines.ts portalName). The Targets cell dropped the mode, so a target limited to push notifications read the same as one that also allows passwordless phone sign-in.
inventory.$commentPolicyRow: What a Policies row states that it left out (ui/surfaces/inventoryTables.ts policiesModel), from facts the coverage engine already reads (coverage/facts.ts). The row read the opposite of what several pinned-baseline policies do: "platforms: all" for a block that excludes Android, iOS, Windows and macOS, "All apps" for a policy excluding an app, "—" for sign-in every time and for a terms-of-use grant, a device filter without its mode, "—" under Exclusions for a policy excluding the Directory Synchronization Accounts role, and "guests" for one excluding only service providers. {include} except {exclude} is targetsExcept; a guest or external type, a platform, a client app type, a flow and a user action are named as the portal names them (roadmap/portalLines.ts portalName).
inventory.$commentRiskRemediation: The Grant cell's word for Graph's riskRemediation grant control (ui/surfaces/inventoryTables.ts CONTROL_WORDS), as the portal's "Require risk remediation" names it. The control had no word, so the pinned baseline's high-risk policies read "Require MFA and riskRemediation" and "Require riskRemediation and strength: …" on screen and in iamai-policies.csv.
inventory.$commentWorkloadSeen: The Detected workloads table's word for a service, from the product's one reading of it (roadmap/workflows.ts serviceReading, the reading Direction's Confirm What You Use asks from): seen in use, not seen where the sources that would show it were read, or not read (pages.connect.scan.gaps.notRead). The table drew "detected" for every service whose goal applies, seen or not, so Azure Virtual Desktop, Azure management and Inforcer read "detected" where Direction said the scan did not see them. Intune is read from the licence, as licensed or not licensed.
inventory.$commentNotAsked: The Detected workloads answer column (Answered in Confirm What You Use) for a service that step never asks about. It asks only about roadmap/directionAnswers.ts SERVICE_KEYS: Azure Virtual Desktop, SharePoint and OneDrive, Azure management, Inforcer and directory synchronization. Copilot, Azure DevOps, Agent identities and Intune read "—" there, the mark for a question with no answer saved, although the step has no question for them.
inventory.$commentEmpty: What an Inventory table says where its section was read and returned nothing (a section not read says notRead). "No Conditional Access policies were read." and "No subscribed licences were read." sounded like failed reads on a tenant that has none, and the blocked-today table fell to the shared "Nothing to show yet.", which gave the reader nothing on a tenant where the records show no one blocked.

alerting.title: Alert on Emergency Account Sign-ins
alerting.why: An alert is how anyone finds out an emergency account was used. It also tells a planned drill apart from access nobody expected.
whatToDo: Send the sign-in logs somewhere they can be queried first: Entra admin center → Entra ID → Monitoring & health → Diagnostic settings → + Add diagnostic setting, pick the sign-in categories, then Send to Log Analytics workspace. That takes at least the Security Administrator role, an Azure subscription and a workspace — or the SIEM you already use.
The accounts are {list:emergencyAccountUpns}. Take each one's object ID from Entra ID → Users; the rule matches on the object ID, not the sign-in name, because a name can be changed under it.

In the Azure portal, as at least a Monitoring Contributor: Monitor → Alerts → + Create → Alert rule. Scope: the workspace. Condition: Signal name Custom log search, Query type Aggregated logs, a SigninLogs query filtered to those object IDs. Alert logic: Static, Greater than, threshold 0.
Give it an action group that reaches a person by email, SMS, push or voice, set Severity 0 - Critical, enable it on creation, and name who answers it.
Test it with one controlled sign-in and confirm the alert arrives. Agree what the responder then does: keep the logs, and decide whether the use was a drill, a real emergency, or neither.
Review ingestion, retention and cost for the monitoring service you use.
doneWhen: A controlled sign-in by an emergency account produced an alert at the monitored destination, and the response owner confirmed receipt.
The response owner knows what happens next: keep the logs, then decide whether the use was a drill, a real emergency, or neither.

hardening.title: Harden Emergency Access
hardening.why: These emergency-access checks were deferred once the minimum ones passed. This is the Cleanup row a scan can close for you: each deferred check has to pass again on the tenant.
whatToDo: {list:hardening}
Do each one, then scan again: the row closes when they pass. A deferral was a decision to wait, never a result, so nothing here counts as done until the scan finds it.
doneWhen: Every deferred emergency access recommendation passes on a scan.

namedExclusions.title: Remove Emergency Accounts Excluded by Name
namedExclusions.why: These policies leave an emergency account out by name as well as through the exclusions group. IAMAI keeps exclusions your tenant already has, so its corrections leave these names in place. The exclusions group should be the only way an emergency account is left out: one group is easier to check and keep right than names spread across policies.
whatToDo: Remove the emergency accounts named under Users → Exclude in {list:namedExclusions}
Before you remove a name, check that the exclusions group holds that account and that the policy excludes the group. The group is what keeps the account out once its name is gone. Then scan again.
doneWhen: A scan finds no On or Report-only policy that excludes an emergency account by name, and the exclusions group keeps each account out.

naming.title: Align Policy Names
naming.why: A naming standard lets the next person find a policy and understand its purpose without opening it. That is what makes the review after this one possible.
whatToDo: Rename {list:renames}
A name that carries its own meaning has a sequence number, the resources it applies to, the response, who it applies to and when. IAMAI proposes names in the convention this tenant already uses.
A Conditional Access policy has no owner field, so put ownership in the name — a team prefix will do — and keep a register elsewhere of who answers for each one.
Renaming changes no Conditional Access evaluation, but scripts or reports that find policies by name may need updating; keep the same policy IDs and settings.
doneWhen: The reviewed policies use the approved names on the next scan.
Verify after the change: tooling that finds these policies still identifies them.

consolidation.title: Review Overlapping Policies
consolidation.why: A tenant is capped at 240 Conditional Access policies, the ones that are off included, so an overlap costs something. It also makes the next change harder to reason about.
whatToDo: Compare the complete settings of {list:overlaps}: scope, exclusions, conditions, controls, risk levels and guest types.

Choose Retain Both and record why when the policies serve different requirements. Otherwise select and save the retained policy and the policies to retire below before disabling or deleting anything. After the approved retirement, scan again so IAMAI can verify the retained policy is enforced and the retired policies are disabled or absent.
Retire by disabling, not deleting: a disabled policy comes back with one switch, while a deleted one can be restored for 30 days and no longer.

Retire a policy only after the remaining one is shown to preserve the required coverage, tested and approved; keep a rollback record. Never remove High-risk coverage because a Medium-only policy exists.
doneWhen: Each overlap has been reviewed: retain both with a recorded reason, or verify the retired policy has a tested replacement preserving its required coverage.

drill.title: Verify Emergency Access
drill.why: Sign in once with each emergency access account's passkey, so you know the way back in works before any policy is turned on.
whatToDo: Follow Verify emergency sign-in in Implementation Tasks for each account named in Tasks Remaining.
Wait 5–10 minutes, then scan to update the plan.
Use Troubleshoot emergency sign-in if a sign-in fails or its evidence does not appear.

steps.title: Prepare Emergency Access Accounts
steps.why: Prepare at least two dedicated emergency access accounts with approved passkeys. These provide administrative access when your normal sign-in is unavailable. Two accounts give you another recovery option if one account or its passkey cannot be used.

who.operatorNote: Use these accounts only for emergency recovery and controlled tests. Do not use them for daily administration.

Enter a unique username, such as emergency-access-primary or emergency-access-secondary, or choose another account name. Select the observed initial domain from the domain list.
Keep the account cloud-only and enabled, then assign Global Administrator through the applicable direct-assignment or PIM route.
Store the initial password securely where authorized staff can retrieve it without signing in to this tenant.

Two marks Microsoft gives for this review: fewer than five Global Administrators, and fewer than ten privileged role assignments in all.

helpDesk: An admin refused by a portal on the everyday account: the role moved; sign in with the admin account.
more.manager: Admin work moves to accounts that do nothing else, so a phished mailbox is not a phished tenant. Without this, every admin inbox is a way in to every setting.

steps.aiFocus: Distinguish direct roles from PIM and keep the staged handover.
steps.$commentCard: The Tasks Remaining cards (ui/surfaces/policyTasks.ts ownCardWordsOf): check null draws no card of the step's own while it is open, because each admin to move is a card of their own (generate.ts, card.admin); satisfied is the Satisfied card's fact (walk list items 2, 14).

card.subject: Administrator accounts
card.satisfied: No admin has a mailbox or Teams licence or signed in to Outlook or Teams in the last 30 days.

steps.taskTitle: Move the role to a separate admin account
steps.$commentProcedure: Move the role to a separate admin account, one task per admin the scan saw on Outlook or Teams (ui/surfaces/sectionThreeTasks.ts separateAdminTasksOf; walk list items 2, 20, 36). Each value is the scan's: {newUpn} and {upn} the new admin account, {everyday} the account that holds the role today, {mail} its email address, {role} one admin role it holds. With no admin to move, the same lines stand with the generic values below, so the procedure reads the same in every state. tapPolicy stands only where the scan read Temporary Access Pass as off; the Active and Eligible lines follow how the role is held and whether the tenant has Privileged Identity Management.

procedure.create: Open [Microsoft Entra admin center](https://entra.microsoft.com/) → **Entra ID → Users → New user → Create new user**, as at least a User Administrator.
procedure.otherEmails: Under **Properties**, set **Other emails** to **{mail}**, so role approvals and service notices reach {name}. Select **Review + create**, then **Create**.
procedure.tap: Open **Entra ID → Users → {upn} → Authentication methods → Add authentication method → Temporary Access Pass**, select **Add**, and copy the pass.
procedure.$commentRegister: The passkey goes on the new admin account through the one Authenticator procedure (content/passkeySetup.ts, owner 2026-09-24), on {name}'s phone; registerPass takes the place of its sign-in prompts line, because this account's only way in is the pass. registerKey is the security-key alternative.
procedure.registerPass: Sign in as **{upn}** with the pass when Authenticator asks.
procedure.registerKey: Using a security key from 1.3's approved list instead: open [Security info](https://mysignins.microsoft.com/security-info) as **{upn}** with the pass, then **Add sign-in method → Passkey → Security key**.
procedure.assign: Open **Entra ID → Roles & admins → {role} → Add assignments**, select **{upn}**, and complete the assignment. If it asks for an assignment type, choose **Active** and **Permanently assigned**.
procedure.assignActive: Open **ID Governance → Privileged Identity Management → Microsoft Entra roles → Roles → {role} → Add assignments**, select **{upn}**. Choose **Assignment type: Active** and **Permanently assigned**.
procedure.assignEligible: Open **Entra ID → Roles & admins → {role} → Add assignments**, select **{upn}**, choose **Assignment type: Eligible**, and select **Assign**.
procedure.test: Sign in to [Microsoft Entra admin center](https://entra.microsoft.com/) as **{upn}** with the passkey and do one task the role is for.
procedure.remove: Then open **Entra ID → Roles & admins → {role}**, select **{everyday}**, and select **Remove assignments**.
procedure.removeEligible: Then open **Entra ID → Roles & admins → {role} → Eligible assignments**, select **{everyday}**, and select **Remove**.
procedure.keep: Keep mail, Teams and files on **{everyday}**; open admin portals with **{upn}** only.
procedure.scan: Return to IAMAI and select **Scan to update the plan**.

steps.title: Restrict Service Accounts to the Trusted Network
steps.why: Restricting user-based service accounts to approved networks can reduce where their passwords are useful. Review all job locations so an infrequent or vendor-hosted process is not missed.

who.none: No service accounts recognised in {tenant}; nothing for this policy to restrict.
evidence: {existingCoverage}

steps.doneEnd: The user-based service accounts in the group can sign in to {tenant} only from the approved trusted network, and every job that uses one has been run from there and recorded.
doneWhen: {policyDoneWhen}

risks.text: A user-based service job outside the approved trusted locations can stop when this policy is enforced. Confirm the execution network and test scheduled or infrequent jobs.
A trusted network that lists a whole ISP range trusts every customer on it.

helpDesk: Inspect the failed job's account, sign-in result and public egress address. Confirm whether the job belongs on an already approved network; adding a new trusted network changes every policy that relies on that trust.
more.manager: Service accounts in the group can sign in only from the approved trusted network, which limits where their passwords are useful. A call made by a service principal is not blocked by a policy scoped to users; covering one takes Conditional Access for workload identities, which Restrict the Directory Sync Service Principal to Its Address builds.

example.policyName: Core - Block - Service accounts outside the trusted network

steps: Network (formerly Conditions → Locations) → Configure: Yes, then Include: Any network or location; Exclude: {trustedLocation}

steps.aiFocus: Include the user-account group and actual workflow evidence. Do not infer service-principal protection or approve a network from sign-in history alone.

whatToDo.lead: Security defaults provide Microsoft's default identity protections on this licence. Check the requirements first, then turn them on if this is the chosen approach.
steps: Entra admin center → Entra ID → Overview → Properties → Manage security defaults.
Tell people they may be asked to set up an authentication method, and give anyone who cannot a way to reach IT support.

doneWhen: The scan reports Security Defaults enabled. Registration readiness is tracked in its own step.
steps.aiFocus: Explain the selected protection model and observed setup gaps. Do not confuse enabling Security Defaults with customizing Conditional Access.

whatToDo.lead: Find what still authenticates the old way, so blocking it later does not break a needed service.
steps: Entra admin center → Identity → Monitoring & health → Sign-in logs, and add the Client app column.
Filter the records you have (up to 30 days) to legacy clients: Exchange ActiveSync, IMAP, POP, SMTP, Other clients.
For every account that appears, find the application behind it and its owner, and ask owners about jobs that run only occasionally.
Record a supported replacement or retirement for each, and test it before blocking access.

doneWhen: The available sign-in records show no successful legacy-client sign-in, or every one left has a named owner and a recorded replacement or outstanding action.
steps.aiFocus: Report the actual evidence window and unresolved dependencies. Do not claim thirty days of coverage when the records do not contain it.

comms.body: Please identify each application, printer or scheduled job that signs in with an older client or username-and-password protocol. Include its account, actual protocol, owner, normal and infrequent run schedules, supported replacement and a delivery or access test window.

whatToDo.lead: App passwords let older applications sign in without an interactive MFA check. Replace each dependency before retiring the credential.
steps: Ask users and application owners which applications still use app passwords, and migrate or retire those applications before removing their credentials.

In Entra admin center, open Entra ID → Users → Multifactor authentication. Select the affected users, open Manage user settings, select Delete all existing app passwords generated by the selected users, then save. Use an authorized Authentication Administrator or Authentication Policy Administrator account.
Separately open the per-user MFA service settings through Conditional Access → Named locations → Configure MFA trusted IPs. Clear the option allowing users to create app passwords, then save.
Disabling creation does not delete existing app passwords. Record the reviewed accounts and the removal and creation-setting checks below.

doneWhen: The reviewed applications no longer depend on app passwords, and the affected app passwords are removed.
Creating new app passwords is disabled where that applies.
steps.aiFocus: Distinguish per-user credentials from tenant method-policy settings. Do not invent a complete app-password inventory from unavailable data.

comms.body: We are retiring app passwords. Please identify any application or job that uses one, arrange its supported replacement and test access with us before removing the credential. Confirm the old app password has been removed and report any failed workflow so we can finish the change.

whatToDo.lead: Keep MFA enforced while you move it from the per-user setting to the replacement you choose.
steps: Entra admin center → Entra ID → Authentication methods → Policies → Manage migration → Migration in progress.
Under Policies, enable every method people actually use, so nobody loses the one they have.
Confirm the replacement MFA protection is enabled and covers each account before changing that account's per-user MFA state.
Entra admin center → Entra ID → Users → Per-user MFA: set an account to Disabled only once its replacement protection is in place; keep the existing setting where no replacement exists.

doneWhen: The tenant reports Migration complete, and no account is left Enabled or Enforced for per-user MFA.
Every account whose per-user MFA was disabled is covered by enabled replacement protection.
steps.aiFocus: Explain why a completed methods migration is not permission to disable every user's MFA state.

whatToDo.lead: Global Administrator has broad authority. Keep it only where the work needs it.
steps: Entra admin center → Identity → Roles & admins → Global Administrator: list active and eligible holders and why each needs the role.
Where a narrower role is enough, assign and test it before removing Global Administrator.
Keep the selected emergency accounts; they are counted here and they are the way back in.
Record the reason for each retained assignment.

doneWhen: Every active and eligible Global Administrator assignment has a recorded purpose, and unnecessary access has been removed while preserving the selected emergency accounts.
The recommended number of administrators is a review aid; a count alone does not prove least privilege.
steps.aiFocus: Treat counts as review signals, not proof. Separate emergency accounts, eligible access and day-to-day administration.

whatToDo.lead: Review guest access with the people who sponsor it, so access that is no longer needed ends through the proper process.
steps: Entra admin center → Identity → Users, filter User type to Guest, and add the Creation time and Last sign-in columns.
For each guest, confirm the sponsor and whether the work still needs the access.
Check pending invitations with whoever sent them; a pending invitation is not automatically obsolete.
Remove access that is no longer needed through your organization's offboarding and retention process.

doneWhen: Every reviewed guest or invitation has a confirmed purpose, or an approved removal that has been completed.
steps.aiFocus: Distinguish pending, inactive and unsupported evidence. Do not infer approval to delete from a missing sponsor field.

whatToDo.lead: Move people from text and voice codes to a stronger approved method, and test it before retiring the old one.
steps: Entra admin center → Entra ID → Authentication methods → Policies: enable the approved replacement method (Microsoft Authenticator or passkeys) for the intended users.
Help people on text message or voice call register the replacement and complete a successful sign-in with it.
Review recovery needs and application dependencies, then disable Text message and Voice call through the approved method-policy change.

doneWhen: Text message and voice call are off in the authentication methods policy, and everyone who used them has registered Authenticator or a passkey.
Each of them signed in with the replacement, and the agreed recovery path is preserved.
steps.aiFocus: Distinguish stronger MFA from phishing-resistant MFA. Do not claim all Authenticator modes are phishing-resistant.

whatToDo.lead: Correct the trusted location's reported problems: every policy that uses it depends on its ranges. Check the enabled policies that use it before saving, then verify the intended traffic and rescan.

doneWhen: Every must-fix check on the trusted location passes on the next scan.
Its ranges match the approved decision.
steps.aiFocus: Explain the failed check, affected location and dependent policies. Trust does not mean every sign-in requirement is bypassed.

whatToDo.lead: Correct the allowed-countries findings: the list decides where the countries policy allows sign-ins. Review the dependent enabled policies before saving, and rescan afterward.
steps: Open Entra admin center, then Conditional Access, then Named locations. Select the location used by your country restriction policy.
Compare its country list with the approved countries shown in this plan. Review policies already using the location before saving a change, because enabled policies use the new list immediately.
Correct the findings shown on this step, then scan again to check the result.

doneWhen: Every must-fix check on the allowed-countries list passes on the next scan.
The named location matches the approved country decision.
steps.aiFocus: Separate approved scope, observed geography and unresolved travel needs.

whatToDo.lead: Correct the pilot group's findings: it decides who tests a new control first, so its members should represent the work the change affects.

doneWhen: Every must-fix check on the pilot group passes on the next scan.
The pilot membership is the approved one.
steps.aiFocus: Explain why each membership or scope issue matters without implying a pilot guarantees a safe wider rollout.

whatToDo.lead: Resolve the service-account findings with each workload owner: a wrong classification can interrupt a job or leave an ordinary account outside important controls.

doneWhen: Every must-fix check on the service accounts passes on the next scan.
The confirmed service-account decisions are reflected in the plan.
steps.aiFocus: Distinguish user-based service accounts from workload identities and explain the actual affected policies.

whatToDo.lead: Correct the authentication strength's reported differences: it is the list of methods its policies accept. Review every policy that references it, keep the same object where supported, then verify and rescan.

doneWhen: Every must-fix check on the authentication strength passes on the next scan.
The strength has the intended combinations.
steps.aiFocus: Include the current and intended combinations, affected policies and TAP where present.

steps.title: Require MFA for Inforcer Access
steps.why: A token for Inforcer needs MFA, whichever app asks for it: Conditional Access follows the resource, not the client. One policy therefore covers every route people take into the application.

evidence: Inforcer application ID: 708861da-226e-4d65-a57a-24128df64524.
{existingCoverage}

doneWhen: {policyDoneWhen}

comms.body: We are reviewing MFA protection for Inforcer access. Please register an approved MFA method for your work account and contact IT if sign-in fails or you need help testing access. Tell IT about any unattended job using a person’s account.

risks.text: A policy scoped to users never reaches a service principal calling Inforcer; a workload identity needs a policy of its own.
One policy per application adds up: a tenant is capped at 240, and Microsoft prefers one policy covering all resources.

helpDesk: Inspect the affected Inforcer sign-in and its Conditional Access result. Check the target application ID, user scope, exclusions and accepted MFA claim.
more.manager: Inforcer user sign-ins require MFA through the app-specific policy.

example.policyName: Core - Require - Inforcer MFA

steps.aiFocus: Explain the exact app target and built-in MFA grant, separating user access from workload identities and installation permissions.
